title: Business continuity: could you keep working for a week without a key system, supplier or site?
short: List the processes that can't stop for a week, give each a written workaround and exercise the plan at least once a year.
answer: This quarter, list the processes that would do serious harm if stopped for a week, set up a crisis team with deputies and a channel outside your own IT, and give each process a one-page workaround. Then run a tabletop and a technical failover at least once a year, and let the measured recovery times decide what to fix next.
audience: IT, security, risk and operations leads in EU organizations of any size, including those under NIS2 or DORA

blocks.title: If you only do five things

items.title: List the processes that can't stop for a week.
items.text: Ask each department what 7 days of downtime would cost, and have management sign off the shortlist. BSI-Standard 200-4 uses such a prefilter to focus the impact analysis[^bsi2004].

items.title: Set up the crisis team first.
items.text: Name a lead, a deputy for each role and a channel that works without your own IT. BSI's entry stage starts here, because a crisis team allows a basic response before any plans exist[^bsi2004].

items.title: Write a workaround for each critical process.
items.text: Describe on one page how it runs on paper, by phone or on spare devices. The NCSC says organizations commonly run with limited or no IT for weeks after a disruptive attack[^ncscrec2].

items.title: Set recovery targets and measure them.
items.text: Give each critical process a maximum tolerable downtime, then recovery time and data loss targets for its systems[^bsi2004]. The backups and ransomware sheets cover restore tests.

items.title: Exercise at least once a year.
items.text: Run a tabletop for decisions and a failover of one top system, and record the times. ENISA advises testing at least annually[^enisatig]; the NCSC warns that many plans fail in practice[^ncscbc].

items.title: What would hurt within a week?
items.text: Ask each unit what a 7-day outage would do to safety, operations, legal and contract duties, reputation and finances[^bsi2004]. Keep those above a threshold agreed with management.

items.title: How long can each process stop?
items.text: Set the maximum tolerable period of disruption, a recovery time objective below it and a recovery point objective for its data[^bsi2004].

items.title: What does it run on?
items.text: List people, sites, IT systems, SaaS, suppliers and data. DORA requires the analysis to cover third-party dependencies and interdependencies[^dora]. Note which share a cloud region or identity provider.

items.title: What is good enough in a crisis?
items.text: Set a minimum service level, such as the share of calls answered within a set time[^enisatig].

items.title: Do your systems meet the targets?
items.text: Compare each target with the last measured restore time. Close the gap, change the workaround or have management accept it.

blocks.title: Keep working without your systems
items: **Check what is critical this month.** Payroll, cash flow, regulatory reporting and peak seasons shift priorities[^ncscrec2]. Note the critical dates.
**Review workarounds for security.** Private email or a shared spreadsheet can add risk. Review each one before use and give it a review date so it doesn't become permanent[^ncscrec2].
**Plan how the data gets back.** Decide early how records kept on paper or in spreadsheets will be reconciled with restored systems[^ncscrec2].
**Keep the inputs on paper.** Print the plan, as ENISA suggests[^enisatig], plus contact lists and price lists, and keep a daily offline export of open orders.

blocks.title: Crisis team, decisions and messages
items: **Agree when to declare a crisis.** Write criteria such as prolonged downtime, several sites hit or likely public scrutiny[^enisatig]. Anyone may escalate; named people declare.

**Decide authority in advance.** Record who makes strategic decisions, your risk appetite and escalation thresholds[^ncscdec], and who may stop deliveries or approve emergency spending. The incident response sheet covers the first hours.

**Prepare messages and channels.** Draft statements for staff, customers and suppliers, and keep channels that work when primary systems are down[^ncscdec]. The EU security laws sheet has the reporting clocks.
**Log decisions and times.** Each time the plan is activated, record decisions, steps and the final recovery time[^enisatig].

blocks.title: What large outages teach
items: **One update can stop all your Windows devices.** A faulty CrowdStrike update on 19 July 2024[^csrca] affected an estimated 8.5 million Windows devices[^msweston], and the manual fix could ask for each BitLocker recovery key[^kb]. Stage such updates, which customers can now control[^csrca], and make sure the help desk can read keys with servers down.

**Sign-in and phones are dependencies.** In AWS's October 2025 outage, Identity Center users in us-east-1 couldn't sign in and callers to Amazon Connect contact centers got busy tones[^aws]. Test emergency access to each cloud console and keep a fallback phone number.

items.title: Can you reach the crisis team?
items.text: Run an unannounced alert test after hours over the backup channel, and tell the works council first. BSI's standard requires alert and crisis staff exercises even at its entry stage[^bsi2004].

items.title: Do the decisions hold up?
items.text: Run a two-hour tabletop: a key SaaS supplier is gone for a week. The NCSC's Exercise in a Box has scenarios[^ncscbc].

items.title: Do the workarounds work?
items.text: Walk through each with its users, then run one for half a day.

items.title: Does failover work under load?
items.text: Run real work on one top system's secondary site, zone or backup. DORA requires most financial entities to test such switchovers[^dora][^rts].

blocks.title: Mistakes that cost the most
items: **Treating recovery time as total downtime.** The recovery time objective runs from declaring the emergency, so detection and decision come off the tolerable downtime first[^bsi2004].
**Planning around one person.** If only one person knows the workaround, the plan fails when they are away. DORA's scenarios include losing a critical number of staff[^rts].
**Trusting the provider's redundancy.** Google says customers must provision failover for zonal resources such as VMs[^gcp]. Ask each critical SaaS provider what its plan leaves to you.
**Testing only the easy parts.** A tabletop alone doesn't show that a top system runs at the backup site. DORA's tests must challenge the plans' assumptions[^rts].

blocks.title: What changed in 2026
items: **A power failure in one zone slowed a cloud region.** On 20 October 2026, generators at Google Cloud's London zone europe-west2-b failed to start; other zones were affected and some failovers failed for lack of capacity[^gcp]. Test failover at full capacity.

**The NCSC published guidance on recovering to minimum viable operations:** the lowest level at which you can operate safely, meet legal duties and keep trust[^ncscrec2]. Set one per critical process.

**Germany's KRITIS umbrella act took effect** on 17 March 2026; the ordinance setting its scope is still a draft[^bbkfaq]. Most registered operators outside IT, telecom and finance have 10 months for a resilience plan[^kritis].

blocks.title: What you can skip
items: **An impact analysis of every process.** BSI's entry stages start with the most time-critical processes and add the rest in later cycles. If you're regulated, include all regulated processes in the first cycle[^bsi2004].
**Certification before the first exercise.** A certificate doesn't show that payroll runs on day three.
**Runbooks for every system.** Write them for the systems critical processes need. Restore the rest from backup in priority order.
**Multi-cloud as the plan.** Running everything twice is costly and rarely tested. First prove failover to a second zone or region.

blocks.title: What this looks like at your size

columns.title: Small team, no security staff
items: Unless regulated, follow BSI-Standard 200-4's reactive entry stage: crisis team with deputies, a 7-day shortlist and one-page workarounds[^bsi2004].
Print the plan, the phone tree and the BitLocker key steps; keep copies with two people at home.
Ask your IT provider and key SaaS suppliers how fast they restore and how they'd reach you without email.

columns.title: Growing, with IT or security staff
items: Have process owners set the targets for the shortlist and management sign them off.
Write runbooks for the top five systems and time one restore or failover each quarter.
Quick machine recovery's cloud remediation is off by default on managed devices[^qmr]: decide whether to turn it on, and stage EDR content updates.

columns.title: Enterprise or regulated
items: NIS2 requires business continuity and crisis management[^nis2]; point 4 of Implementing Regulation 2024/2690 details it for cloud, managed service and other digital providers[^nis2ir].
Under DORA, test yearly; all but microenterprises add cyberattack and switchover scenarios and a crisis management function[^dora].
Exercise the loss of a cloud zone and region, and check which SaaS suppliers share them.

First draft, based on BSI-Standard 200-4, Implementing Regulation 2024/2690 and ENISA's guidance on it, DORA and its ICT risk management standards, NCSC guidance on disruptive attacks and the providers' reports on the CrowdStrike, AWS and Google Cloud outages.
